query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory high‐entropy alloys (HEAs), the unusually high hardness and strength are mainly governed by the dominance of edge dislocations whose motion is strongly hindered by lattice distortions induced by the multi‐principal element composition. In contrast to conventional BCC metals where screw dislocations control plasticity, the atomic size mismatch in HEAs increases edge dislocation density and their pinning, effectively raising the resistance to plastic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, refractory BCC high-entropy alloy (for example, NbTaTiV or CrMoNbV) with significant lattice distortions and a microstructure exhibiting a high prevalence of edge dislocations.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the alloy composition to increase or decrease atomic size mismatch and lattice distortion (for instance, by adjusting the concentration of larger or smaller atomic species) while maintaining the single-phase BCC structure.
generation.conditions: Mechanical deformation tests (e.g., nanoindentation and tensile tests) at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (up to ~1073 K) performed under controlled loading conditions. A conventional BCC alloy with minimal lattice distortion and predominantly screw dislocation activity will be used as a baseline for comparison.
generation.structural_mediator: The density and mobility of edge dislocations, which are strongly affected by local lattice distortions introduced by the compositional complexity.
generation.mechanism: Increased lattice distortions resulting from significant atomic size mismatches in HEAs promote the formation and effective pinning of edge dislocations. These edge dislocations act as robust barriers to plastic deformation by raising the energy barrier for dislocation motion, thereby enhancing hardness and yield strength relative to systems governed by screw dislocation mechanisms.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with larger lattice distortions (i.e., greater atomic size mismatch) will exhibit an increased density of pinned edge dislocations, resulting in higher hardness and yield strength compared to alloys with lower lattice distortion. The deformation behavior will show a slower rate of softening with increasing temperature compared to conventional BCC alloys where screw dislocations dominate.
generation.baseline: A conventional BCC alloy engineered to have minimal lattice distortion and, consequently, plasticity dominated by screw dislocations, which should display lower hardness and a more temperature-sensitive flow behavior.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase, refractory BCC high-entropy alloys with significant atomic size mismatch. It may not hold in alloys with FCC structures, multiphase microstructures, or where other mechanisms (such as precipitation or grain boundary strengthening) are dominant.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between the degree of lattice distortion and the extent of edge dislocation pinning is not fully defined; moreover, the transition temperature ranges and exact scaling of dislocation contributions with composition may vary and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of refractory BCC HEAs with systematically varied levels of lattice distortion (via controlled compositional adjustments) while ensuring a consistent single-phase microstructure. In parallel, prepare a conventional BCC alloy with low lattice distortion. Use transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and in situ neutron diffraction to quantitatively assess the populations of edge versus screw dislocations in each alloy. Conduct nanoindentation and tensile tests at room and elevated temperatures to measure hardness, yield strength, and deformation behavior.
measurements: Edge and screw dislocation densities (using TEM and neutron diffraction)
Yield strength and strain rate sensitivity from tensile tests
Lattice parameter and distortion levels (via XRD or dilatometry)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If increasing the calculated lattice distortion (via compositional modification) does not result in a corresponding increase in edge dislocation density and does not lead to higher hardness and yield strength compared to the baseline conventional BCC alloy, or if the deformation mechanism remains dominated by screw dislocations despite high lattice distortion, then the hypothesis is falsified.

AbstractIn this study, high-pressure torsion (HPT) processing is applied to the as-cast Al0.5CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) for 1, 3, and 5 turns. Microstructural observations reveal a significant refinement of the second phase after HPT processing. This refinement effect is influenced by the number of processing turns and the distance of the processing position from the center. As the number of processing turns or the distance of the processing position from the center increases, the fragmentation effect on the second phase becomes more pronounced. The hardness of the alloy is greatly enhanced after HPT processing, but there is an upper limit to this enhancement. After increasing the number of processing turns to 5, the increase in hardness at the edge becomes less significant, while the overall hardness becomes more uniform. Additionally, the strength of the processed alloy is significantly enhanced, while its ductility undergoes a noticeable decrease. AbstractEnergy efficiency is motivating the search for new high-temperature (high-T) metals. Some new body-centered-cubic (BCC) random multicomponent “high-entropy alloys (HEAs)” based on refractory elements (Cr-Mo-Nb-Ta-V-W-Hf-Ti-Zr) possess exceptional strengths at high temperatures but the physical origins of this outstanding behavior are not known. Here we show, using integrated in-situ neutron-diffraction (ND), high-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM), and recent theory, that the high strength and strength retention of a NbTaTiV alloy and a high-strength/low-density CrMoNbV alloy are attributable to edge dislocations. This finding is surprising because plastic flows in BCC elemental metals and dilute alloys are generally controlled by screw dislocations. We use the insight and theory to perform a computationally-guided search over 107 BCC HEAs and identify over 106 possible ultra-strong high-T alloy compositions for future exploration.Subject terms: Mechanical engineering, Mechanical properties, Computational methods The strength in BCC high-entropy alloys is associated with the type of mobile dislocations.
